whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should consider the Technical Architect Evaluation?

personas.label: CTA candidates ready for the first stage
personas.description: You hold both architect credentials and need to pass this assessment before booking the review board.

personas.label: Senior architects checking readiness
personas.description: You want to know whether your architecture and presentation skills meet the board’s expectations.

personas.label: CTA mentors and practice leads
personas.description: You coach candidates and want a clear picture of what this assessment measures.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Technical Architect Evaluation?
examDifficulty.summary: This is the first part of the CTA assessment, not a standard multiple-choice exam. You review a scenario, develop an architecture, and discuss it with a Salesforce evaluator. The assessment checks readiness before you commit to the larger review-board fee.
bullets: No multiple-choice paper. You explain a solution to a scenario and defend your design.
Earn the prerequisites first. Both Application Architect and System Architect must be active.
It is a gate to the board. Passing allows you to proceed to the review board.
Fee: External sources report a fee of about US$1,500 for this stage, with the board charged separately. Confirm current pricing with Salesforce.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can read a scenario, produce a sound design within the available time, and explain your decisions without notes. If you have not practised defending a design aloud, do so before booking.

examFormat.heading: Technical Architect Evaluation format
examFormat.intro: This is a scenario discussion with an evaluator, not a written question paper. Prepare for the following:
bestWayToPass: Read carefully before designing: Many errors come from solving a different problem than the scenario describes.
Use a repeatable structure: Cover data, security, integration, release lifecycle, and licensing so you do not skip an area under pressure.
Explain alternatives: State what else you considered and why you chose your approach.
Practise under a time limit: Rehearse completing and presenting designs within the time available.

practiceQuestionsIntroSuffix: , practice scenario-style thinking and technical architecture concepts for the Architect Evaluation.

certificationCard.description: Stage one of the CTA assessment. You work through an enterprise scenario with a Salesforce evaluator, design a solution and discuss it. Passing opens access to the review board.

keyConcepts.h2: Technical Architect Evaluation: concepts to prepare

blocks.heading: Purpose of the evaluation
blocks.body: The evaluation is a smaller readiness stage before the full review board. It uses a hypothetical company, its goals, systems, and constraints, and one evaluator rather than a panel. Passing lets you book the board. Take it seriously: the ability to understand requirements and defend architecture decisions is tested again at the board.

blocks.heading: Read the scenario closely
blocks.body: Separate requirements and constraints—such as residency rules, existing systems, or budget—from background details. A common mistake is designing for an expected problem rather than the one described. List each requirement and check it against your design before presenting so you can show how it is covered.

blocks.heading: Build a complete design
blocks.body: A strong design covers the data model, record access, integrations, release approach, and required licences. Prefer standard platform features when they fit. If you choose custom work, explain what requirement makes it necessary. Keep the solution proportionate: extra products or components create cost and questions that need a reason.

blocks.heading: Explain and defend decisions
blocks.body: For each major choice, identify the requirement it meets, another option you considered, and the trade-off you accepted. Acknowledge limitations and respond to challenges with evidence. Adjust when an objection is sound, while explaining your reasoning when you retain a choice. Neither reflexively giving in nor refusing to reconsider shows good judgement.

blocks.heading: Prepare with complete practice scenarios
blocks.body: Practise with full scenarios rather than reviewing topics in isolation. Set a timer, create a complete design, and present it to someone who will ask you to explain your choices. Use a consistent outline, record yourself, and notice where you avoid making a clear decision. Rehearse reading, designing, and defending several times before booking.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Technical Architect Evaluation
scenarioTips.intro: A clear and accurate design matters more than adding complexity. Solve the scenario as written and explain your reasoning.

blocks.heading: Show requirement coverage
blocks.body: List the stated requirements and connect each one to part of the design. This prevents avoidable gaps.

blocks.heading: State assumptions
blocks.body: When a detail is unclear, say what assumption you are using and continue. Make assumptions visible.

blocks.heading: Draw for clarity
blocks.body: Use a readable diagram that you can explain. Label integrations and data flows.

blocks.heading: Explain each major choice
blocks.body: Cover the need, your decision, the alternative, and the trade-off for each significant design choice.

blocks.heading: Rehearse with a timer
blocks.body: Practise producing and explaining a complete design within the time allowed.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate is preparing to book the Technical Architect review board. What does the Evaluation stage confirm first?
options: To replace one of the two required architect credentials
To issue the CTA credential before the final board stage
To verify readiness before the candidate commits to the review board
To evaluate Apex coding skill under a fixed time limit
sampleQuestions.explanation: It is the readiness gate the candidate must clear before scheduling the board; passing it does not itself award the CTA credential.
whyWrong: It does not replace a prerequisite credential.
The CTA credential is awarded after the review board, not at this stage.
The assessment is not an Apex coding test.

sampleQuestions.question: A scenario requires customer data to remain in the EU. The proposed design puts it in a US-hosted system and does not address the requirement. What is the main issue?
options: Only the project cost may change
The design ignores a stated constraint
The evaluator must ask before it matters
Data location is solely an infrastructure team concern
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scenario constraints are requirements. Ignoring a data-residency requirement is a serious design gap.
whyWrong: The issue is compliance and requirement coverage, not just cost.
The candidate should address stated constraints without waiting for a prompt.
Data residency is an architecture decision that must be handled in the design.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate discovers that one requirement is ambiguous. What should they do?
options: Stop the assessment until someone clarifies it
State a reasonable assumption and continue the design
Leave the requirement out of the solution
Design a separate solution for every possible interpretation
sampleQuestions.explanation: An explicit assumption lets the evaluator understand the basis for the design and shows how the candidate handles uncertainty.
whyWrong: The candidate is expected to proceed rather than stop.
Omitting a requirement leaves a gap in the design.
Covering every interpretation can create an unnecessarily broad solution.

sampleQuestions.question: Which explanation best demonstrates sound architectural judgement?
options: Defer every design choice to the client without analysis
Select the most advanced available technology without comparing fit
Add many Salesforce products to demonstrate platform breadth
Explain the requirement, chosen approach, and trade-off
sampleQuestions.explanation: The assessment looks for the reasoning behind a choice, including the need it serves and the trade-off it creates.
whyWrong: The architect still needs to explain the design rather than defer every decision.
Technical sophistication does not make an option appropriate by itself.
Unneeded components add complexity and need justification.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate proposes custom work for a need that a standard Salesforce feature appears to meet. How may this be assessed?
options: As acceptable whenever the custom solution works
As a sign of strong engineering in every situation
As a concern unless a specific requirement makes the standard feature unsuitable
As the better choice because custom code is always easier to change
sampleQuestions.explanation: Standard capabilities are preferred when they meet the need. Custom work requires a clear justification.
whyWrong: Custom work carries maintenance costs that should be considered.
Judgement is more important than adding technical complexity.
Flexibility alone does not justify the extra cost and support burden.

sampleQuestions.question: Which credentials must be active before a candidate takes this stage?
options: A completed Trailhead superbadge and project portfolio
Active Application Architect and System Architect credentials
Three years of continuous employment in a Salesforce architect role
Administrator and Platform Developer I credentials
sampleQuestions.explanation: Both Application Architect and System Architect are prerequisites for the CTA path.
whyWrong: A superbadge is not one of the CTA prerequisites.
There is no stated three-year employment requirement.
Administrator by itself does not meet the prerequisites.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should candidates practise producing a design under time pressure?
options: It checks whether candidates can finish a sound design on time
Salesforce recommends skipping product documentation
Candidates receive the scenario and its requirements before booking
Timed practice guarantees a passing score
sampleQuestions.explanation: Candidates at this level are expected to know the platform. They need to organize and explain a complete design within the available time.
whyWrong: Reading remains useful, but timing and structure are also part of the assessment.
The scenario is not provided in advance.
Practice can improve readiness but cannot guarantee a result.

sampleQuestions.question: An evaluator raises a reasonable concern about an integration choice. How should the candidate respond?
options: Discuss the concern and revise the design if the reasoning supports a change
Rewrite the scenario requirement so that the original choice appears correct
Withdraw the choice immediately without considering the objection
End the discussion and refuse to revisit the decision
sampleQuestions.explanation: Thoughtful adjustment shows that the candidate can evaluate new information. Stubbornness and immediate capitulation both weaken the defence.
whyWrong: The scenario requirements do not change during the discussion.
A decision should be reconsidered, not abandoned without thought.
The candidate is expected to communicate and defend the architecture.

sampleQuestions.question: Which set of topics belongs in a complete architecture design?
options: Cover only the integrations and systems shown in the architecture diagram
Address only the screens and user interactions
Describe only the data objects, fields, and relationships
Cover data, access, integration, delivery lifecycle, and licensing
sampleQuestions.explanation: A complete design considers all of these areas, so a consistent outline helps prevent omissions.
whyWrong: Integration is one part of the architecture, not the whole design.
An enterprise design covers more than the interface.
A data model alone does not address security, integration, delivery, or licensing.

sampleQuestions.question: How does the evaluation fit into the CTA process?
options: It removes the review board from the CTA process
It is scheduled only after a candidate passes the review board
It is another name for the same board assessment
Passing the evaluation allows the candidate to book the review board
sampleQuestions.explanation: The evaluation comes first and gates the final review board; they are separate stages.
whyWrong: Candidates still need to complete the board.
The required order is evaluation followed by the board.
They are distinct assessments with separate fees.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate has a strong design but cannot explain all of it before time runs out. What should they practise?
options: A consistent presentation outline and timed rehearsal
Relying on design quality without explaining it
Arguing that the scenario was unfair
Adding more detail to the design
sampleQuestions.explanation: Candidates must communicate the design within the allotted time. A repeatable structure helps cover the necessary areas.
whyWrong: An unexplained design cannot be evaluated fully.
Time limits are part of the assessment.
More detail can make it harder to finish on time.

sampleQuestions.question: What should a candidate do with the scenario requirements before presenting?
options: Map every stated requirement to the design and show where it is met
Address only the technical requirements and leave business needs aside
Repeat the requirement list without connecting it to the design
Assume the evaluator will remember all scenario requirements
sampleQuestions.explanation: Mapping each requirement to the design shows directly that the solution addresses the scenario.
whyWrong: Business requirements matter as well as technical ones.
Restating requirements without showing coverage does not demonstrate a solution.
The candidate is responsible for showing how the design meets the requirements.

sampleQuestions.question: What kind of scenario is used in this stage?
options: A live Salesforce org that the candidate must configure
A hypothetical company with goals and constraints
The candidate’s current employer
A set of multiple-choice questions
sampleQuestions.explanation: CTA assessments use hypothetical enterprise scenarios to evaluate architecture decisions.
whyWrong: This is not a hands-on configuration exercise.
The candidate’s employer is not the basis of the scenario.
The stage is scenario-based, not multiple choice.

sampleQuestions.question: A design adds middleware that the scenario may not need. What should the candidate be prepared to do?
options: Treat it as an automatic failure whenever middleware appears
Say the middleware will reduce time spent discussing the design
Explain the need for the component and its cost or complexity
Claim middleware is required for every enterprise integration
sampleQuestions.explanation: Every component should serve a requirement. The candidate should justify its purpose and account for its costs or complexity.
whyWrong: An unnecessary component is a concern, but one choice is not automatically a failure.
The addition may create more questions rather than shorten the discussion.
Middleware is an architectural option, not a universal requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: Which rehearsal is most useful before the evaluation?
options: Review architecture diagrams without presenting or discussing them
Re-read prerequisite exam guides without practising a scenario
Create a timed design and explain it to someone who asks questions
Memorize platform limits without rehearsing design decisions
sampleQuestions.explanation: The assessment requires designing and defending a solution under time pressure, so practise the full activity aloud.
whyWrong: Passive review does not practise the presentation and defence.
Those guides prepare candidates for prerequisite exams, not the full scenario discussion.
Platform limits matter, but memorizing them does not practise architecture defence.
